items.text: 11 May 1973 — Sheaves, continued
Torsors (principal homogeneous sets) under a group $G$ in $\mathbf{Sets}$: $E\ne\varnothing$, $G\times E\to E$ simply transitive.
E\to\{*\}\ \text{ is an epimorphism (surjective)}
Monomorphism = limit statement: $E\to F$ mono iff $E=E\times_F E$ (diagonal).
E\xrightarrow{\ \Delta\ }E\times_F E\ \ \text{iso}
Epimorphism: only through direct limits — the square is cocartesian.
\begin{array}{ccc}E&\to&F\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\\ F&\to&F\sqcup_E F\end{array}\qquad F\sqcup_E F=F\ (\text{iso})
Torsors in sheaves
A sheaf of groups $G$ acting on a sheaf of sets $E$; simple transitivity means
G\times E\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }E\times E,\qquad (g,e)\mapsto(ge,e)
Not « $E(U)\neq\varnothing$ for all $U$ »: rather the map to the final sheaf $X$ is an epimorphism.
E\to X\ \text{epimorphism}\iff E_x\neq\varnothing\ \ \forall x\in X
So $E$ is a torsor iff each stalk $E_x$ is a $G_x$-torsor.
Epimorphism of sheaves is not surjective on sections: $E(U)\to X(U)$.
Stalks non-empty = local sections. A global section exists iff the torsor is trivial:
E(X)\neq\varnothing\iff E\simeq G\ \text{(acting on itself by left translation)}
Non-trivial torsors exist in sheaves, not in $\mathbf{Sets}$ — the interesting case.
Transport of structures
Define structures in sheaves by copying the set-theoretic definition diagrammatically: fibre products, amalgamated sums.
Theorems proved in sets about such constructions hold in sheaves over any space.
Proof: statements say that arrows are mono / epi / iso, or that pairs of arrows agree: check on stalks.
Fibre functors commute with these limits and are jointly conservative, so check on fibres, i.e. in $\mathbf{Sets}$.
Chevalley's IHÉS seminar (1958-59): a year spent on such structures — « a bad mess ». We keep the idea only.
Fields and integral domains
Not describable by inverse limits alone: a field. Every non-zero element invertible.
1\neq 0;\qquad x\neq0\Rightarrow x \text{ is a non-zero-divisor}
Not expressible with finite inverse limits: need direct limits.
Sheaf of rings $K$. Cheating answer: « $K$ is a domain iff its stalks are ». Better: a subsheaf $K'$ and an epimorphism.
$K'\subset K$: elements by which left and right multiplication are injective.
Axiom: every element is in $K'$ or is zero.
K'\sqcup X\ \xrightarrow{\ (\text{incl},\,0)\ }\ K\ \ \text{epimorphism}
It remains to define $K'$ by inverse limits.
K\longrightarrow \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K,K),\qquad f\in K(U)\ \mapsto\ (x\mapsto fx)|_U
$\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(K,L)(U)=\operatorname{Hom}(K|_U,L|_U)$ is a sheaf.
$K'_{\ell}$: those $f$ whose left multiplication is injective — a local property, hence a subsheaf; likewise on the right.
K'=K'_{\ell}\cap K'_{r}
Exercise (next time): express $K'$ through inverse limits.
Sheaves of domains or fields are seldom used so far.
Generators
Logical foundations: large categories, small subcategories; universes — SGA 4, vol. 1, exposé I.
A set of objects $(Z_i)$ of $C$ is a generating set.
E\hookrightarrow F\ \text{mono and}\ \forall i:\ E(Z_i)\xrightarrow{\sim}F(Z_i)\ \Longrightarrow\ E\xrightarrow{\sim}F
Enough to test subobjects on the test objects $Z_i$.
Equivalent (in a topos): the family of functors $E\mapsto E(Z_i)$ is conservative.
\forall i:\ E(Z_i)\xrightarrow{\sim}F(Z_i)\ \Longrightarrow\ E\xrightarrow{\sim}F\quad\text{for any arrow}
Proof: factor into epi followed by mono.
E\twoheadrightarrow F'\hookrightarrow F,\qquad E(Z_i)\to F'(Z_i)\hookrightarrow F(Z_i)
Reduce to the cases of mono (given) and epi.
An epimorphism which is a monomorphism is an isomorphism (as in sets).
$E\to F$ mono iff the diagonal is an isomorphism:
E\xrightarrow{\ \Delta\ }E\times_F E\ \ \text{mono; check it on each } Z_i
E(Z_i)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }E(Z_i)\times_{F(Z_i)}E(Z_i)
Used: fibre products, epi-mono factorisation, bimorphism = iso.
Generators of $\operatorname{Top}(X)$
The open sets $U\in\mathcal O$, viewed as sheaves (étale spaces over $X$):
U(V)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(V,U)=\begin{cases}\{*\}&V\subset U\\ \varnothing&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
$\mathcal O$ is a small family and it generates.
\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Top}(X)}(U,E)=E(U)
If $E(U)\to F(U)$ is bijective for all $U$, then $E\to F$ is an isomorphism: tautological.
Abelian sheaves
$\operatorname{Ab}(X)$: abelian group objects of $\operatorname{Top}(X)$ = functors $\mathcal O^{\circ}\to\mathbf{Ab}$ that are sheaves of sets.
An abelian category: kernels, cokernels as for abelian groups.
Inverse limits: as for sheaves of sets. Direct limits: ad hoc, via filtering ones.
Filtering direct limits commute with the forgetful functor to sets, and are exact.
(F_i)_{i\in I}\mapsto\varinjlim_i F_i\quad(I\text{ filtering})\ \text{ exact}
Enough injectives
An abelian sheaf $I$ is injective if every map from a subobject $F\subset G$ into $I$ extends to $G$.
F\hookrightarrow G,\quad F\to I\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\, G\to I
A (Grothendieck) abelian category with exact filtering direct limits and a small generating family has enough injectives.
Generators for $\operatorname{Ab}(X)$: the free abelian sheaf on each $Z_i$ (free group defined via direct limits).
Use also: characterising topoi (later).
Modules
$A$ a sheaf of rings: $\operatorname{Mod}(A)$ — abelian, exact filtering direct limits, small generating family, hence enough injectives.
Homological algebra works: injective resolutions, $\operatorname{Ext}$ groups and sheaves, cohomology.
Not enough projectives in general: filtering inverse limits are not exact; the category is not self-dual.
Technical digression on generators ends.
